title: Walk a Nested List Flat
statement:
A nested list holds integers and other nested lists, to any depth, for example [1, [2, [3, []]], 4]. Build an iterator that hands out its integers one at a time, in the order they appear when the list is read left to right.

  • NestedIterator(nested) wraps the list. Here the list is a plain array (a Python list): each element is either a number or another array.
  • hasNext() returns true if at least one integer has not been handed out yet. Calling it several times in a row must not skip anything.
  • next() returns the next integer. It is only called when one remains.

Empty lists, even deeply nested ones, contain no integers and are skipped.

Tests are a list of operations and their arguments; the first operation creates the iterator. The expected output has one entry per operation (null for the constructor).

examples.why: Read left to right: 5 and 6 from the first sublist, then 7, then 8 from two levels down. The trailing [] adds nothing, so after 8 nothing is left.
Lists that contain only empty lists hold no integers. hasNext has to look inside them before answering.

constraints: next is only called when hasNext would return true
hints: The easy way is to flatten everything in the constructor. It works, but it does all the work up front even if only one value is read. Can you produce values only when asked?
Recursion would handle the nesting, but an iterator has to stop in the middle and resume later. Which structure can hold "where I am in each open list"?
Keep a stack of (list, index) frames. Before answering hasNext, move forward: pop finished lists, step into sublists, and stop when the top frame points at a number.

explain.intuition:
Reading a nested list in order is a depth-first walk. A recursive function would do it, but an iterator must pause after each value and pick up later. So make the call stack explicit: a stack of frames, each holding one open list and the position inside it. The top frame is the list you are reading right now.

The trick is to do all the moving inside one helper. Before hasNext or next answers, advance until the top frame points at an integer or the stack is empty. Finished lists are popped, sublists are pushed as new frames. Empty lists simply get pushed and popped again, so they never produce anything. This is the same idea as walking a DOM tree with a manual stack instead of recursion.
steps: settle(): while the stack is not empty, look at the top frame. If its index is past the end, pop it.
If it points at a sublist, move the index forward and push a new frame [sublist, 0].
If it points at a number, stop: that number is next.
hasNext() calls settle() and returns whether the stack is non-empty. next() calls settle(), then returns the number at the top frame and moves its index forward.
pitfalls: Answering hasNext by checking only whether the current list has elements left. [[], [[]]] has elements but no integers.
Making hasNext consume a value. Calling it twice in a row must give the same answer and lose nothing.
Pushing a frame for the sublist without first advancing the parent's index. When the sublist finishes, the parent would push it again forever.

complexity.time: O(1) amortized per call; every list is pushed and popped once

solutions.title: Flatten up front
solutions.idea: Do a recursive walk in the constructor and keep a flat array plus a cursor. Simple, but uses O(total) memory and does all work at once.

solutions.title: Lazy stack of (list, index) frames
solutions.idea: An explicit depth-first walk that pauses. A helper advances until the top frame points at a number; both methods call it first.

followups: Write the same iterator as a generator function (function* in JavaScript, yield in Python). What does the runtime keep for you?
Add a peek() method that returns the next value without consuming it.
